**Prologue**

*

In the forgotten corners of the world—places ancient and isolated—strange, terrible things happen.

They happen around Hua Jiunan.

Or maybe Hua Jiunan is one of those things.

After all, he was born from a corpse.

**1: When the Dead Come Knocking**

Strange, terrible things always happen in ancient, isolated places.

And those things happen to Hua Jiunan.

Or maybe Hua Jiunan is part of them.

Because he was born from a corpse.

---

Nine-Ditch Village sat deep in the frozen north, buried among a hundred thousand mountains.

The cold was brutal. Snow and wind owned the place, all year round.

Even in the early 1980s, the villagers lived almost entirely cut off from the outside world.

Every decision in the village — big or small — went through Deaf Granny and Old Man Li.

Deaf Granny was a Spirit-Caller.

Since ancient times, there's been a saying in China: "Southern Sorcery, Northern Spirits."

Southern Sorcery meant the Daoist exorcists of Maoshan.

Northern Spirits meant the Spirit-Callers of the north.

A true Spirit-Caller kept the "Four Pillars and Eight Beams" — twelve spirit families — enshrined in their home.

The Four Pillars were: Hu (Fox), Huang (Weasel), Chang (Snake), and Qingfeng.

Qingfeng were the vengeful ghosts of those who died violent deaths.

The Eight Beams were eight specialized offices: Sweep, See, String, Guard, Reach Heaven, Return to Earth, Block, and Scout.

(Their duties will be explained in due time.)

Deaf Granny wasn't actually deaf. Her maiden name was Zhang, and her full married name was Wang Zhang-shi.

They called her "Deaf" — or rather "Dragon" — because her patron spirit was a snake, and snakes are sometimes called "little dragons."

Deaf Granny lost her husband early. Two of her three sons died in accidents. Only the third son stayed by her side.

Everyone in the village just called him Wang San.

Today was the fifteenth day of the seventh lunar month — the Ghost Festival.

As soon as the sun went down, Deaf Granny told Wang San to bolt the courtyard gate. She wanted to turn in early.

The living and the dead don't mix. A collision between the two was bad news for everybody.

But before she could even lie down, a violent pounding shook the courtyard door.

Not knocking. Pounding. Heavy. Hollow.

Wang San was pissed. He threw on his patched-up cotton coat and stomped toward the gate, cursing under his breath.

"I'm comin', I'm comin'! Would ya quit that poundin'?"

"You fixin' to die or somethin', bangin' on folks' doors this time of night!"

The gate swung open.

A gust of icy wind hit him in the face.

The figure standing outside tilted forward like a felled log and crashed face-first into the courtyard — stiff, straight, completely limp.

Only a body-shaped dent remained in the thick snow.

"Well I'll be damned — did they up and die on us?"

Wang San hauled the person out of the snow and hollered toward the house:

"Mama! Get out here and take a look!"

Deaf Granny's heart had already jumped when she heard that first knock.

She ran to the side room where the spirit families were enshrined, grabbed the Spirit-Binding Rope, and sprinted back outside.

This wasn't some mythical immortal-binding treasure from the old legends.

A Spirit-Binding Rope was braided by the Spirit-Caller themselves — using willow branches, their own hair, and ancient copper coins.

Then it was soaked in pine resin mixed with incense ash for three years.

After three years, it was washed, dried, and laid at the feet of the spirit shrine.

The rope was seven feet long, pitch black, and warded against ghosts and evil.

Deaf Granny ran, her mind screaming:

*Ghost Festival. Ghost knocking at the door. Bad luck. Bad luck.*

At the same time, Old Man Li from next door heard the commotion and came running.

He was an outsider. He'd only moved to the village three years ago.

But when the villagers found out he was a veteran who'd fought off the Japanese devils, they treated him with deep respect.

The two elders squinted in the snow-reflected moonlight and saw Wang San holding up a woman with a face as white as bone.

She looked frozen solid. Her whole body was stiff as a board.

Wang San only had to grip her by the shoulders and she stood there, propped up like a mannequin.

In that state, the bulge of her belly was impossible to miss.

She was pregnant. Ready to deliver.

Deaf Granny's voice cut through the frozen air like a blade.

"The Eighth Master of the Chang family sits this shrine. I suggest you leave — now."

The woman's head cranked toward them, joint by joint, with a slow, grinding creak.

Her eyes were dead gray. When she spoke, every word came out separate, scraped raw from a throat that sounded like rusted machinery.

"Pl-eeease."

"S-s-save... my... child."

Wang San, thick-headed as a brick, didn't register anything strange. He just nodded enthusiastically.

"You need someone to deliver that baby, don't ya? My mama only does exorcisms, she ain't no midwife. For that kinda thing, you want Zhang's wife down at the east end."

"Aw heck, you can barely walk. I'll go fetch her for ya."

Deaf Granny saw her son heading out the gate and shouted:

"San'er — stop right there! She's dead!"

Wang San jumped. He scrambled back and put himself between his mother and the woman.

"Mama, don't go scarin' me like that!"

Old Man Li frowned deeply and stepped up beside Wang San.

"Deaf Granny... you sure?"

Deaf Granny stared hard at the woman, not blinking.

"Old woman's eyes ain't gone yet. I know what I'm seein'."

"You two look close. That thing ain't breathin'."

Old Man Li studied the woman.

She wasn't lying.

The three of them were standing in the snow. Every breath they took puffed white steam into the frozen air.

The woman across from them? No steam. Not a wisp.

And the snow that had settled on her face wasn't melting. It had frozen solid.

The woman heard Deaf Granny's words. Something snapped.

Her eyes rolled back in her skull until only the whites showed.

She dragged her legs forward, stiff and straight, charging straight at the three of them.

"I'm NOT dead!"

"I'm NOT dead!"

"Please — please save my baby!"

**2: The Living Corpse**

Deaf Granny's eyes blazed with fury.

"You ungrateful creature! Begone!"

She cracked the Spirit-Binding Rope like a whip, the blow landing hard across the woman's body.

A shriek tore through the night. Black smoke curled up from the woman's skin.

But even through the pain, she kept crawling forward, inch by inch — driven by only one thing: Deaf Granny had to save her child.

Uncle Li watched, brow furrowed. "Deaf Granny... she talks. She yells. She's got a shadow. You sure she's dead?"

Deaf Granny's voice dropped low. "Living Corpse."

"She's dead, she just don't know it yet. The only thing keepin' her goin' is pure stubborn need."

Uncle Li's face went grim. "She's dead, sure. But the baby in her belly — dead or alive?"

Deaf Granny kept her eyes locked on the woman. "Alive."

"If that baby was gone, her drive'd be gone too. She'd drop right here — two bodies, one soul gone bad. That's a Death-in-Childbirth Demon. Nasty business."

"Mother and child both carryin' scissors, huntin' for someone to take their place. Every new mother in these parts'd be in danger."

Uncle Li took a long, hard drag on his pipe. "Well, if that baby's still breathin', we can't just stand by."

"Dressed plain as she is, she's poor folk same as us. We help."

Hearing this, the woman tried to drop to her knees in gratitude — but her body had gone stiff. She couldn't bend.

Deaf Granny had a good heart under all that bark. Hearing Uncle Li's words, she relented.

"Now listen here, Li. You best be ready. If we try to save that baby and fail... mother and son'll turn into vengeful spirits right then and there."

Uncle Li let out a rough laugh. "You tell me — how mean were them Japanese soldiers? I still chopped 'em down one by one with this blade."

"You think a ghost's scarier than a Jap?"

"Only thing is, I don't know the first thing 'bout birthin'. That part's all on you."

Deaf Granny looked at the fire still burning in the old man's eyes and cracked a small smile.

"Deliverin' a dead woman's baby... can't say I've done that before, neither. Let's hope nothin' goes sideways."

"The Spirit Guardians hold court inside the house — no evil can get in there. So we'll do this in the yard."

Deaf Granny sent Wang San to fetch basins of hot water. She draped black cloth to screen off a space in the snow-covered yard.

Then — the Spirit-Binding Rope in her hand moved on its own.

It twisted and curled across the snow, tracing out words in crooked strokes:

THIS ONE — GREAT DANGER.

Deaf Granny's breath caught. If her own Spirit Guardians were warning her... this thing before them was more terrifying than she'd imagined. This Living Corpse wasn't what it seemed.

Uncle Li saw the look on her face. He wasn't about to let Deaf Granny's household walk into danger.

"Third," he said to Wang San, "go borrow Old Liu's donkey cart. I'm takin' this woman to the town hospital."

Wang San nodded quick. "I'll go with you, Uncle. Safer that way."

"Both of you, stop right there!" Deaf Granny's voice cut through the night. "You think sendin' somethin' halfway between dead and alive to the town is smart? You wanna kill more folks?"

"I'll deliver this baby myself. Third — you get back. Stay nearby and wait for my word. Li — you're my assistant."

With a life on the line, there was no room for modesty. And the patient was already dead besides.

Uncle Li agreed at once. "Alright. You tell me what needs doin', I'll do it."

Deaf Granny turned to the woman. "You remember your birth date and hour?"

The woman blinked. Some memories had already slipped away. Slowly, she pieced it together.

Deaf Granny listened — and her face went pale.

"Yin year. Yin month. Yin hour. Extreme Yin Constitution."

"On tonight of all nights — Ghost Festival. We're in for it now."

But there was no time to dwell. The woman's face was twisting, distorting. Black, foul-smelling pus began seeping from the corners of her eyes. A low, rattling laugh bubbled from her throat. Her long hair thrashed in the night wind.

This meant the baby was in danger — could die any moment.

And if that happened, the mother would turn into a full-blown demon right then and there. Mother and son, raging through this tiny village. A catastrophe.

"Third!" Deaf Granny's voice rang sharp. "Fetch the Great Seal!"

The Great Seal was the mark of a Spirit Medium's rank — and a powerful tool against evil.

Wang San felt the danger in the air and ran without another word.

Deaf Granny thought fast. "Li. Go get your broadsword. I sure hope you wasn't braggin' about that blade havin' drawn blood."

Uncle Li laughed, big and bold. "Deaf Granny, if you can call them Japanese soldiers human, then my sword's tasted plenty. Hundred'd be on the low side. You just watch."

Wang San came running back, the Great Seal raised high. "Ma, why'd you send Uncle Li for his sword? Is it really that special?"

Deaf Granny was already loosening the woman's clothes. "Special don't cover it. That sword's killed men. If a blade's taken a hundred lives, we call it a Hundred-Kill Blade. A righteous man wields it — and nothing unclean dares come close."

Just then, Uncle Li returned. The red-tasseled saber was slung across his back — and the sight of him was pure menace. Pure authority.

The dark, creeping dread in the air... had already started to pull back.
